questions.body: In Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm for detecting a cycle in a singly linked list, how fast do the two pointers move, and what indicates a cycle?
questions.keyPoints: Slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps; if they meet (slow == fast), a cycle exists.

options.text: Slow moves 1 step, Fast moves 2 steps; if `slow == fast` at any non-null node, a cycle exists.
options.explanation: If a cycle exists, the distance between fast and slow decreases by 1 on every step within the loop, guaranteeing they meet in O(N) time and O(1) space.

options.text: Slow moves 2 steps, Fast moves 4 steps; if fast reaches null, a cycle exists.
options.explanation: Reaching null indicates a terminated linear list with NO cycle.

options.text: Both move 1 step in opposite directions.
options.explanation: Singly linked lists can only be traversed forward.

options.text: Slow stores visited node addresses in a Hash Set.
options.explanation: Floyd's algorithm uses two pointers to achieve O(1) space without a hash set.

questions.body: Once Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet inside a cycle, how do you locate the exact start node of the cycle?
questions.keyPoints: Reset one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time; their meeting point is the cycle start.

options.text: Reset one pointer to the head of the list and advance both pointers 1 step at a time; their meeting point is the cycle entrance.
options.explanation: Mathematically, the distance from head to cycle entrance equals the distance from the intersection point to the cycle entrance along the loop. Moving both at speed 1 brings them together at the entrance.

options.text: Reverse the linked list from the meeting point.
options.explanation: Reversing a cyclic list corrupts pointers and enters an infinite loop.

options.text: Count the number of nodes in the cycle and divide by 2.
options.explanation: Cycle length alone does not identify the head offset.

options.text: Advance the fast pointer until it hits null.
options.explanation: Inside a cycle, fast will never hit null.

questions.body: What pointers are required to reverse a singly linked list in-place iteratively in O(N) time and O(1) space?
questions.keyPoints: Three pointers: prev (null), curr (head), and next.

options.text: Three pointers: `prev` (initialized to null), `curr` (head), and `next` (to preserve the rest of the list before redirecting `curr.next = prev`).
options.explanation: The loop executes: `next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;` until `curr == null`, returning `prev` as the new head.

options.text: Two pointers swapping node values like an array.
options.explanation: Swapping values in singly linked lists is inefficient and violates pointer re-wiring.

options.text: A stack storing all node values.
options.explanation: A stack takes O(N) auxiliary space, whereas pointer reversal achieves O(1) space.

options.text: Recursion with a global hash table.
options.explanation: Iterative reversal requires only 3 pointers in O(1) space.

questions.body: How can you find the middle node of a singly linked list in a single pass?
questions.keyPoints: Fast & slow pointers: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

options.text: Advance `slow` by 1 node and `fast` by 2 nodes; when `fast` reaches the end (`null` or `fast.next == null`), `slow` will be at the middle.
options.explanation: Because fast travels at twice the speed of slow, when fast reaches the end of the list, slow has traversed exactly half the distance.

options.text: Count total nodes in pass 1, then traverse to N/2 in pass 2.
options.explanation: That requires two passes; fast/slow does it in a single pass.

options.text: By checking if `node.next.next == node`.
options.explanation: That checks for a 2-node cycle, not list midpoint.

options.text: By calculating the average of all node memory addresses.
options.explanation: Heap memory allocations are not contiguous or monotonic.

questions.body: What is the time complexity to merge two sorted singly linked lists of sizes M and N into a single sorted list?
questions.keyPoints: O(M + N) time by comparing heads and splicing pointers.

options.text: O(M + N) time and O(1) auxiliary space
options.explanation: By comparing the current nodes of both lists and splicing `next` pointers using a dummy head node, all elements are merged in linear time without creating new nodes.

options.text: O(M * N) time and O(1) space
options.explanation: Linear merge does not use nested loops.

options.text: O((M + N) log(M + N)) time
options.explanation: Because both input lists are already sorted, comparison takes linear time, not sorting time.

options.text: O(log(M + N)) time
options.explanation: Every node must be visited to rewire pointers.

questions.body: What data structures are combined to implement an LRU (Least Recently Used) Cache with O(1) `get` and O(1) `put` operations?
questions.keyPoints: A Hash Map and a Doubly Linked List.

options.text: A Hash Map (for O(1) key-to-node lookups) and a Doubly Linked List (for O(1) node removal and insertion at head/tail).
options.explanation: The hash map stores keys mapped to doubly linked list nodes. The doubly linked list maintains usage order: moving accessed nodes to the head and evicting from the tail are both O(1) pointer updates.

options.text: An array and a Binary Search Tree.
options.explanation: BST lookups and mutations take O(log N) time, not O(1).

options.text: A Stack and a Queue.
options.explanation: Stacks and queues do not support O(1) arbitrary key lookup or middle-element removal.

options.text: A Min-Heap and a dynamic array.
options.explanation: Heap operations take O(log N) and arbitrary updates take O(N).

questions.body: What problem does a Monotonic Decreasing Stack solve in O(N) total time?
questions.keyPoints: Next Greater Element problem.

options.text: Next Greater Element (finding the first element larger than the current element to its right or left).
options.explanation: A monotonic decreasing stack keeps elements in descending order. When an element greater than stack top arrives, top elements are popped and have their next greater element resolved, visiting each index at most twice.

options.text: Detecting cycles in a directed graph.
options.explanation: Cycle detection in directed graphs uses DFS with recursion stack or Kahn's algorithm.

options.text: Calculating prefix sums in O(1) time.
options.explanation: Prefix sums are stored in simple arrays.

options.text: Balancing an AVL tree.
options.explanation: Tree rotations balance AVL trees.

questions.body: How does a Stack evaluate whether a string containing brackets `()[]{}` is valid and correctly nested?
questions.keyPoints: Push opening brackets; on closing bracket, pop and verify matching pair.

options.text: Push opening brackets onto the stack; on encountering a closing bracket, pop the top element and check if it forms a matching pair; stack must be empty at the end.
options.explanation: Because the last opened bracket must be the first one closed (LIFO), a stack mirrors the nesting structure directly in O(N) time and O(N) space.

options.text: Count total open vs total closed brackets; if counts match, it is valid.
options.explanation: Matching counts fails on ordering violations like `)(` or `([)]`.

options.text: Sort the string and check if pairs are adjacent.
options.explanation: Sorting destroys the nesting sequence.

options.text: Queue all brackets and dequeue in pairs.
options.explanation: Queues are FIFO; nested matching requires LIFO (Stack).

questions.body: How can a FIFO Queue be implemented using two LIFO Stacks (`inStack` and `outStack`) with O(1) amortized `dequeue`?
questions.keyPoints: Enqueue pushes to inStack; dequeue pops from outStack (if empty, transfer all from inStack to outStack).

options.text: Push new items to `inStack`; on dequeue, pop from `outStack`; if `outStack` is empty, pop all elements from `inStack` and push them to `outStack` (reversing their order to FIFO).
options.explanation: Each element is transferred between stacks at most once, making each element undergo 1 push to inStack, 1 pop from inStack, 1 push to outStack, and 1 pop from outStack -> O(1) amortized time per operation.

options.text: Transfer all elements back and forth between stacks on every single enqueue and dequeue.
options.explanation: Transferring back and forth on every operation degrades performance to O(N) worst case.

options.text: Store elements in stack 1 and their negative values in stack 2.
options.explanation: Values do not determine FIFO ordering.

options.text: Use stack 1 for even numbers and stack 2 for odd numbers.
options.explanation: Queue ordering is strictly temporal (arrival sequence).

questions.body: How can a Stack support `push`, `pop`, `top`, and retrieving the minimum element (`getMin`) all in O(1) time?
questions.keyPoints: Maintain an auxiliary stack tracking the minimum value at each stack depth.

options.text: Maintain an auxiliary `minStack` alongside the main stack, pushing `min(val, minStack.top())` onto `minStack` during each push operation.
options.explanation: The auxiliary stack mirrors the height of the main stack, recording the current minimum element up to that depth so `getMin()` is a simple O(1) peek on `minStack`.

options.text: Scan the stack with a loop during every `getMin()` call.
options.explanation: Scanning takes O(N) time, violating the O(1) requirement.

options.text: Keep the stack sorted at all times.
options.explanation: Keeping a stack sorted violates the LIFO contract and requires O(N) insertion.

options.text: Store all elements in a single integer variable.
options.explanation: A single integer cannot represent an arbitrary stack of items.

questions.body: How does a circular queue of fixed capacity `C` differentiate between an empty queue and a completely full queue when using `head` and `tail` pointers?
questions.keyPoints: Maintain an explicit size counter, or allocate capacity C+1 where (tail + 1) % capacity == head indicates full.

options.text: Either maintain an explicit `size` counter, or allocate an array of capacity `C + 1` and designate `(tail + 1) % capacity == head` as full.
options.explanation: Without a size counter or an extra slot, `head == tail` is ambiguous because it represents both an empty queue and a full queue.

options.text: By checking if `tail < head`.
options.explanation: In a circular queue, `tail < head` occurs naturally when the tail wraps around.

options.text: By scanning the array for null values on every operation.
options.explanation: Scanning takes O(N) time, destroying O(1) queue guarantees.

options.text: A circular queue cannot be full.
options.explanation: Fixed-capacity circular queues have a definite maximum size.

questions.body: What data structure enables solving the 'Largest Rectangle in Histogram' problem in optimal O(N) time?
questions.keyPoints: Monotonic increasing stack of bar indices.

options.text: A Monotonic Increasing Stack of bar indices.
options.explanation: When encountering a bar shorter than stack top, the popped bar's height is bounded on the right by the current index and on the left by the new stack top, allowing O(N) area computation.

options.text: A binary search tree.
options.explanation: BST achieves O(N log N) which is suboptimal compared to stack's O(N).

options.text: A 2D Dynamic Programming matrix.
options.explanation: 2D DP takes O(N^2) time and space.

options.text: A FIFO queue.
options.explanation: Histograms require LIFO backtracking of heights.

questions.body: How can the N-th node from the end of a singly linked list be removed in a single pass?
questions.keyPoints: Fast and slow pointers with fast advanced N steps ahead of slow.

options.text: Advance `fast` pointer `N` steps ahead; then move both `fast` and `slow` together until `fast.next == null`; `slow.next` will be the node to delete.
options.explanation: Maintaining a constant gap of N nodes between fast and slow ensures that when fast reaches the final node, slow sits directly before the node to be removed.

options.text: Reverse the list, delete the Nth node from front, then reverse back.
options.explanation: That requires three passes across the list instead of a single pass.

options.text: Convert the linked list into an array in pass 1.
options.explanation: That takes O(N) auxiliary memory; two pointers takes O(1) space.

options.text: Traverse backward from the tail using `node.prev`.
options.explanation: A singly linked list does not have `prev` pointers.

questions.body: Two singly linked lists A and B intersect at a common node. What is the elegant two-pointer approach to find the intersection node in O(N + M) time and O(1) space?
questions.keyPoints: When pointer A reaches end of list A, redirect to head of list B; when B reaches end, redirect to head of A.

options.text: Pointer A traverses list A then switches to head B; pointer B traverses list B then switches to head A. Both travel `length(A) + length(B)` and collide at the intersection node (or null).
options.explanation: By having both pointers traverse `a + c + b` and `b + c + a` total nodes, any difference in prefix length is equalized, causing them to meet at the exact intersection node in pass 2.

options.text: Compare node values starting from head.
options.explanation: Values can match by coincidence; intersection is based on reference/pointer identity.

options.text: Reverse both lists and find where they diverge.
options.explanation: Reversing intersecting lists breaks the shared tail structure.

options.text: Binary search through the node addresses.
options.explanation: Linked lists are not sorted or indexable in O(1).

questions.body: What operations does a `Deque` (Double-Ended Queue) support in O(1) time?
questions.keyPoints: Push and pop at both the front and back ends.

options.text: Insertion and removal at both the front and the back ends (`pushFront`, `popFront`, `pushBack`, `popBack`).
options.explanation: A Deque generalizes both stacks and queues, allowing O(1) push and pop operations from both ends.

options.text: Arbitrary index insertion in O(1) time.
options.explanation: Middle insertions in deques take linear O(N) time.

options.text: Sorting elements in O(1) time.
options.explanation: Sorting any collection takes at least O(N log N).

options.text: Priority-based automatic reordering.
options.explanation: Priority ordering is the function of a Priority Queue / Heap.

questions.body: How does a Monotonic Deque solve the 'Sliding Window Maximum' problem of window size K in O(N) total time?
questions.keyPoints: Deque stores indices of elements in decreasing order; front always holds the maximum of the current window.

options.text: The deque stores indices of elements in monotonically decreasing value order; elements outside the window are popped from the front, and smaller elements are popped from the back before inserting.
options.explanation: Because smaller elements that arrive before larger elements can never be the maximum again, popping them ensures the front of the deque always contains the current window's maximum index in amortized O(1) per step.

options.text: By calculating the maximum using a max-heap in O(N log K) time.
options.explanation: A max-heap takes O(N log K) time; the monotonic deque achieves strictly linear O(N) time.

options.text: By scanning the K elements for each window position.
options.explanation: Naive scanning takes O(N * K) time.

options.text: By sorting each window in-place.
options.explanation: Sorting each window takes O(N * K log K).

questions.body: How does a Stack evaluate an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (Postfix, e.g. `['2', '1', '+', '3', '*']`)?
questions.keyPoints: Push operands; on operator, pop two operands, apply operator, and push result back.

options.text: Push operands onto the stack; when an operator is encountered, pop the top two operands, evaluate the operation, and push the result back onto the stack.
options.explanation: In postfix notation, operators follow their operands. Popping two values (`b = pop(), a = pop()`) and evaluating `a OP b` resolves expressions linearly in O(N) time with no parentheses needed.

options.text: Convert the expression into prefix notation first using recursion.
options.explanation: Postfix can be evaluated directly with a stack without conversion.

options.text: Push operators and pop numbers.
options.explanation: Operands are pushed; operators trigger evaluation.

options.text: Read the expression from right to left.
options.explanation: Postfix is evaluated from left to right; prefix is evaluated right to left.

questions.body: How can a linked list where each node contains an additional `random` pointer be deep-copied in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space (without a hash map)?
questions.keyPoints: Interweave cloned nodes directly next to original nodes (A -> A' -> B -> B'), set random pointers, then decouple lists.

options.text: Insert cloned nodes directly adjacent to their originals (`orig -> clone -> orig.next`), copy random pointers via `orig.next.random = orig.random.next`, then decouple the interwoven lists.
options.explanation: By weaving the cloned nodes into the original list, the clone's random target is always directly adjacent to the original's random target (`orig.random.next`), removing the need for an O(N) hash map.

options.text: Use a two-dimensional adjacency matrix.
options.explanation: An adjacency matrix takes O(N^2) space.

options.text: Sort the nodes by memory address.
options.explanation: Address sorting does not reconstruct arbitrary random pointer associations.

options.text: Random pointers cannot be cloned without an O(N) hash map.
options.explanation: The interweaving technique is the standard O(1) auxiliary space solution.

questions.body: What is a Skip List, and what average time complexity does it achieve for search, insertion, and deletion?
questions.keyPoints: A probabilistic multi-level linked list that achieves O(log N) search, insert, and delete.

options.text: A probabilistic multi-level linked list that achieves average O(log N) time for search, insertion, and deletion by skipping over elements using express forward lanes.
options.explanation: Skip lists maintain multiple layers of linked lists where higher layers act as express lanes. With geometric coin-toss promotion, search and updates match balanced BST performance (O(log N)) with simpler concurrency.

options.text: A linked list that skips every odd-indexed node, achieving O(1) search.
options.explanation: Search in a skip list is logarithmic O(log N), not constant O(1).

options.text: A circular doubly linked list used exclusively for CPU cache lines.
options.explanation: It is an algorithmic data structure commonly used in databases (e.g. Redis Sorted Sets).

options.text: A singly linked list where deletion is disabled.
options.explanation: Skip lists fully support deletion in O(log N) time.

questions.subtopic: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
questions.body: When flattening a multilevel doubly linked list where nodes may have a `child` pointer to another doubly linked list, how does a Stack or Depth-First Search achieve the correct order?
questions.keyPoints: Traverse nodes; when a child is present, push next node onto stack, link child as next, and resume.

options.text: When a node has a child, push its `next` node onto a stack, rewire `curr.next` to `child`, and upon reaching the child tail, pop and attach the saved `next` node.
options.explanation: This mirrors a preorder depth-first traversal, ensuring that child sub-lists are spliced completely before returning to the original level's next sibling.

options.text: All children must be moved to the end of the root list in FIFO queue order.
options.explanation: Multilevel flattening requires depth-first order so a child immediately follows its parent.

options.text: By converting all child pointers to null and discarding the sub-lists.
options.explanation: Discarding sub-lists destroys data.

options.text: By sorting the nodes based on child pointer values.
options.explanation: Flattening preserves hierarchical structural order.
